strengths: The problem is important and timely: reducing the quadratic attention cost of video diffusion transformers is directly relevant to practical video generation deployment.

The paper proposes a coherent post-training framework with two useful components: selective layer-wise replacement of quadratic attention by linear attention, and an anytime distribution matching objective for recovering quality during transfer.

The empirical results support the main direction: on Wan 1.3B, replacing 16/30 attention layers gives reported 1.43x end-to-end speedup with VBench scores close to FlashAttention2, and longer-frame tests show 1.52-2.00x speedups.

The ablations are informative. Tables 2-4 study the replacement target, selective transfer, regularization, and ADM objective; the large drop without Lreg and with manual/heuristic replacement supports the need for progressive learned selection.

The method is potentially useful because it is post-training and data-free in the sense of relying on teacher-generated trajectories rather than original curated video datasets, making it more plausible to apply to existing models than full retraining.
The paper is mostly clear in its high-level motivation and connects the method to existing linear attention, sparse attention, and distribution matching literature.
weaknesses: The experimental scope is narrow. All main results appear to use a single base model, Wan 1.3B, and there is no evidence on larger video models, other architectures, image-to-video settings, different resolutions, or substantially longer videos beyond the frame-number latency plot. This limits confidence that the layer replaceability patterns and ADM behavior generalize.

The quality gains over strong baselines are small and mostly benchmark-metric based. For example, Ours is close to FlashAttention2 and SVG2 across the eight VBench dimensions, and the 4-step distilled model drops on several quality metrics. There is no human evaluation or stronger perceptual analysis to support claims such as “lossless acceleration” and “exceptionally high visual quality.”

The method comparison is incomplete for the central claim of post-training linearization. The paper compares mainly to sparse-attention accelerators, while the most relevant linear or mixed sparse-linear post-training baselines are only discussed or treated as concurrent. This makes it harder to isolate how much of the contribution is superior linear-attention transfer versus choosing a different efficiency tradeoff.

There is a technical ambiguity in the selective transfer formulation. The text defines r near 1 as preserving quadratic attention and r near 0 as selecting linear attention, but Eq. (9) minimizes (sum ceil(r_l) - target)^2 while target is described as the number of layers replaced by linear attention. If target=16 for 30 layers, the equation seems to enforce 16 quadratic layers rather than 16 linear layers. This may be a notation error, but it is material for reproducibility and understanding the optimization.

The ADM derivation is under-specified in the main paper. The score estimator relation in Eq. (13), the use of the current model to estimate its own score, and the assumptions under rectified flow need more detail to judge correctness. Several important derivations and implementation choices are deferred to an appendix that is not present in the provided manuscript.

The “data-free” training protocol is not fully reproducible. The paper says it collects 50K input-output pairs from teacher trajectories and omits conditions for simplicity, but for text-to-video models the prompt/condition distribution is crucial. The source or generation of training prompts, sampling schedule, storage details, and exact hyperparameters are not sufficiently specified.

Efficiency reporting is somewhat incomplete. The paper reports end-to-end latency on a single H100 but does not give memory use, attention-kernel details, training cost in GPU-hours for the full pipeline, or latency/quality tradeoffs under optimized kernels. Since the achieved non-distilled speedup is moderate, these details matter for practical usefulness.

Some presentation and citation issues reduce confidence. For example, the reference cited for linear attention in one place appears to be a quantization paper, and many key claims point to an appendix for visual artifacts, catastrophic distillation drops, grid-search details, and alpha ablations that is not included.

strengths: The paper targets an important bottleneck in video diffusion models: quadratic self-attention at long spatiotemporal sequence lengths. A post-training route to partial linear-attention replacement would be useful if robustly validated.

The proposed framework is coherent at a high level: layer-wise mixed attention with learnable replacement scores, regularization to make the scores binary, and a distribution-matching objective over intermediate sampling timesteps are plausible components for reducing degradation during linearization.

The experiments include relevant efficiency/quality tradeoffs on Wan1.3B, with ablations for the target number of replaced layers, the selection strategy, the regularizer, and the ADM objective. These ablations support the claim that naive MSE tuning and naive/manual layer replacement are inadequate.

The reported main model gives a practical, if moderate, end-to-end speedup of about 1.25-1.50x while keeping VBench scores close to the FlashAttention2 baseline, and the few-step distilled variant provides a much larger latency reduction.
weaknesses: There appears to be a consequential inconsistency in the selective-transfer constraint. The text defines r=1 as preserving quadratic attention and r=0 as choosing linear attention, but Eq. (9) constrains sum ceil(r) toward target while target is described as the number of layers replaced by linear attention. For N=30 and target=16, this equation would encourage 16 quadratic layers, not 16 linear layers. The layer set later reported for LINVIDEO contains 16 replaced linear layers, so either the equation or the description is wrong. This undermines technical clarity and reproducibility.

The empirical scope is narrow for a CVPR-level systems/methods claim. The method is evaluated essentially on a single base model, Wan1.3B, with no demonstration across other video diffusion architectures, model scales, resolutions, prompt sets, or image-to-video/text-to-video variants. This makes the claimed general framework insufficiently established.

The evidence for preserved generation quality is not fully convincing. The improvements over FlashAttention2 or sparse baselines on VBench are often very small and could be within metric noise, while some metrics degrade. There is no human preference study, no FVD/CLIP-style complementary evaluation, no seed variance/confidence intervals, and limited qualitative evidence in the main paper.

The main acceleration result is modest for the non-distilled method: around 1.43x at the chosen setting, despite replacing 16/30 attention layers. The paper acknowledges no specialized linear-attention kernel is used, but the practical usefulness of partial linearization remains less compelling without memory measurements, longer-sequence stress tests, or wall-clock training/inference cost comparisons over a broader regime.

The method is called data-free, but it requires collecting 50K teacher trajectory input/output pairs and training for 3K steps on 8 H100 GPUs, plus extra DMD2 training for the fastest model. This is dataset-free rather than cost-free, and the paper does not quantify the teacher-sampling and post-training compute relative to alternatives.

Several important details are deferred to an appendix that is not present in the provided manuscript, including derivations, grid-search details, more implementation details, additional qualitative examples, and failure/artifact examples. This materially affects reproducibility and the ability to verify the ADM derivation and training procedure.

The novelty is incremental relative to existing ingredients: Hedgehog-style linear attention, DMD/distribution matching, straight-through binary gating, and layer selection/rounding are combined for video DM linearization. The paper would need stronger validation to compensate for the relatively compositional nature of the contribution.

Baseline coverage and fairness are not fully satisfying. The paper excludes some relevant efficient-attention methods due to resource or shape constraints, does not compare directly with the most closely related post-training sparse-linear attention direction beyond a textual discussion, and gives limited detail on whether sparse baselines were tuned comparably for this exact model and setting.

The writing contains overclaims such as “lossless acceleration” and “far outperforms” that are not supported by the small metric differences and observed drops in some settings. There are also presentation issues and notation problems, including inconsistent/scattered definitions, possible attention scaling typos, and references to appendix material unavailable in the submission.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely bottleneck: reducing quadratic attention cost in large video diffusion models without full retraining. A data-free post-training route for converting selected layers to linear attention would be practically useful if reproducible.

The core idea is well motivated. The observation that layer replaceability varies substantially, and the resulting selective transfer mechanism, are sensible and supported by targeted ablations against manual and heuristic layer choices.

The anytime distribution matching objective is a meaningful technical contribution for this setting. The paper provides ablations showing clear gains over naive output matching and final-distribution DMD-style matching, as well as a training-efficiency advantage over using an extra score approximator.

Empirical results on Wan 1.3B are encouraging: the method roughly preserves VBench and VBench-2.0 quality while yielding reported 1.25-2.00x latency speedups, and the target-layer ablation usefully exposes the quality/speed tradeoff.
The paper is generally readable, with clear motivation, a coherent training pipeline, and relevant comparisons to sparse-attention acceleration baselines.
weaknesses: The evaluation is still somewhat narrow for the strength of the claims. Most evidence is on a single base model, Wan 1.3B, with automated VBench/VBench-2.0 metrics and limited qualitative examples. There is no human evaluation or broader validation across other video diffusion architectures, resolutions, or prompt distributions.

The 15.92x speedup result is partly confounded by few-step distillation, not just the proposed linear-attention post-training. This is useful practically, but the paper should more carefully separate gains from attention replacement versus gains from reducing denoising steps.

Several reproducibility details are under-specified in the main manuscript. The method is called data-free, but for a conditional text-to-video model it is unclear what text conditions/prompts are used when collecting the 50K teacher trajectory pairs. Training hyperparameters, prompt sources, target selection details, and baseline implementation settings appear to rely on an appendix that is not present in the provided manuscript.

There is a technical/notation inconsistency in the selective-transfer constraint: r=1 denotes preserving quadratic attention and r=0 denotes linear attention, yet Eq. (9) constrains sum ceil(r) to equal the target number of linearized layers. This seems reversed relative to the text and the reported 16 replaced layers, and should be corrected for clarity and reproducibility.

The comparison set omits or only briefly discusses the most directly related linear/post-training mixed-attention direction, such as SLA, and focuses mainly on sparse-attention baselines. This limits how conclusively the paper establishes superiority over alternative linearization strategies.

Some reported gains over FlashAttention2 on quality metrics are very small and may be within metric noise; the paper does not report variance over seeds/prompts or statistical uncertainty. Claims such as 'lossless acceleration' should therefore be softened or supported with repeated evaluations.

There are presentation and citation issues, including an apparent incorrect citation for DMD2 in the implementation section, plus several claims deferred to an appendix not included here. These do not undermine the main idea but weaken confidence in the exact experimental recipe.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical bottleneck in video diffusion transformers: quadratic self-attention cost at long spatiotemporal sequence lengths. The proposed post-training approach is useful because it targets existing pretrained video DMs rather than requiring full pretraining of a linear-attention architecture.

The method is technically coherent and has two clear components: selective transfer for deciding which layers to linearize, and anytime distribution matching for preserving the teacher model distribution along the sampling trajectory. The layer-wise replaceability observation is well motivated and supported by diagnostic results.

The empirical evaluation is reasonably strong: results are shown on both Wan1.3B and Wan14B, at 480p and 720p, with VBench and VBench-2.0 metrics. The reported latency gains of 1.43x to 1.71x over FlashAttention2 while maintaining similar benchmark quality are practically meaningful.

Ablations are useful and targeted. The paper studies the number of replaced layers, compares selective transfer against manual and heuristic selection, evaluates the regularizer, and compares ADM with MSE and DMD-style objectives. These ablations support the main design choices.

The paper is generally clear and includes implementation details in the appendix, including data collection scale, batch sizes, training steps, hardware, hyperparameters, and evaluation sampling protocol.
weaknesses: The claimed preservation of quality is supported mainly by automatic video benchmarks and a small number of qualitative examples. For video generation, VBench-style metrics can miss temporal artifacts, prompt fidelity failures, and perceptual degradation. The paper would be stronger with human preference studies or more direct temporal consistency/error analyses.

The method is described as efficient and data-free, but the post-training cost remains substantial: 3K steps on 8 H100s for Wan1.3B and 32 H100s for Wan14B, plus collecting 50K teacher trajectory pairs. This is much cheaper than pretraining, but not lightweight, and the paper could more carefully quantify the break-even point between training cost and inference savings.

The ADM derivation relies on estimating the linearized model's score using the model currently being trained. This is plausible for a multi-step flow model, but the approximation and its optimization details are not fully justified. It is also unclear how sensitive ADM is to timestep discretization, solver choice, stop-gradient choices, and mismatch between one-step perturbed samples and full generated trajectories.

The baseline comparison has some gaps. The authors exclude SLA because of kernel/hardware constraints and exclude some sparse-attention methods due to training cost or shape limitations. These choices are understandable, but they weaken the claim of broadly outperforming prior post-training or mixed-attention approaches. The comparison also lacks memory usage and scaling results as sequence length or video duration increases.

The 15.9x to 20.9x speedup numbers are largely due to combining with 4-step DMD2 distillation, not solely the proposed linear-attention conversion. The paper distinguishes this, but the headline could be read as attributing most of the gain to LINVIDEO itself.

Reproducibility is only partial from the manuscript. Important details such as exact prompt sets, selected training timesteps, code/kernel implementation, random seeds, and full evaluation scripts are not included, and no release plan is evident from the paper. Given the scale of the models, independent reproduction may be difficult.

strengths: The problem is important and timely: reducing the quadratic attention cost in video diffusion models is highly relevant for practical video generation, and the paper targets strong open models rather than toy architectures.

The proposed combination of selective layer replacement and an anytime distribution matching objective is a coherent practical framework. The layer-replaceability observation is plausible and supported by ablations showing that layer choice matters substantially.

The empirical section includes nontrivial experiments on Wan 1.3B and 14B, reports latency, compares against several sparse-attention baselines, and evaluates on both VBench and VBench-2.0. The reported 1.43x-1.71x speedups with limited metric degradation are potentially useful.
The ablations are helpful: target replacement count, selective transfer, regularization, and ADM are each tested, and the results generally support the design choices.
weaknesses: The paper overstates some claims. Calling the method 'lossless' is not fully supported: several VBench/VBench-2.0 dimensions drop, the 4-step variant has clearer quality degradation, and the reported differences may be within benchmark noise without confidence intervals or repeated-run variance.

The practical speedup is modest for the core linear-attention conversion, despite the paper emphasizing O(n) attention. Since many layers remain quadratic and no long-sequence scaling study is provided, the asymptotic claim is not strongly connected to demonstrated end-to-end behavior.

The evaluation relies almost entirely on automatic video-generation metrics and a few qualitative examples. There is no human preference study, no temporal artifact quantification beyond selected examples, and limited evidence that visual quality is preserved under diverse prompts or failure cases.

The comparison set is incomplete and somewhat selective. SLA is excluded because of kernel constraints, methods requiring more training are excluded, and the paper does not fully disentangle algorithmic gains from implementation choices. The DMD2 speedups also conflate attention replacement with a large reduction in denoising steps.

The 'data-free' framing is potentially misleading: the method still uses prompts from OpenVid and 50K teacher-generated trajectories. It avoids real video data, but it is not free of data generation, prompt distribution assumptions, or substantial teacher inference cost.

The training cost is high for a post-training method: 8 H100s for Wan 1.3B and 32 H100s for Wan 14B, plus teacher trajectory collection and optional distillation. The paper does not provide a full cost-benefit analysis versus the latency saved at deployment.

Some technical assumptions behind ADM are under-justified. In particular, using the current model to estimate its own score along samples derived from teacher trajectories is plausible but not rigorously validated; the derivation does not fully address approximation error or off-trajectory behavior.

Reproducibility is only moderate. The paper gives many implementation details, but exact prompt lists, training data generation procedure, code, seeds, hardware/kernel settings, and benchmark variance are not sufficient to confidently reproduce the reported close metric differences.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely bottleneck in video diffusion models: quadratic attention cost at long sequence lengths. A post-training route to partial linear attention is practically useful, especially for open pretrained models such as Wan.

The proposed framework is technically coherent overall. Selective transfer is a sensible mechanism for layer-wise replacement, and the ADM objective is well motivated by the shortcomings of direct output matching and final-distribution-only distillation.

The empirical evidence is fairly strong: results are shown on both Wan1.3B and Wan14B, with end-to-end latency measurements on H100 and evaluation on VBench and VBench-2.0. LINVIDEO improves latency by 1.43-1.71x while mostly preserving automated quality scores, and the 4-step distilled variant gives much larger speedups with moderate degradation.

The ablation studies are useful and targeted. The paper separately examines the target number of linearized layers, selective transfer versus manual/heuristic selection, the regularization term, and ADM versus MSE/DMD-style alternatives. These ablations support the main design choices rather than only reporting final numbers.
The method has good potential utility because it does not require access to the original training dataset and can be applied as a post-training modification to large video generators.
weaknesses: There is a concerning inconsistency in the formulation of the target constraint. The paper defines r as the quadratic-attention score and says linear attention is selected when the rounded score is 0, but Eq. (9) constrains sum ceil(r) to equal target while the text says target is the number of linearized layers. For Wan1.3B, target=16 and the selected set contains 16 linearized layers, which would imply sum ceil(r)=14 for a 30-layer model. This may be a notation error, but it affects technical clarity and reproducibility of the core selection mechanism.

The evaluation relies heavily on automated VBench/VBench-2.0 scores. These are useful but imperfect proxies for video quality, temporal artifacts, prompt following, and perceptual preference. There is no human study, no side-by-side preference test, and limited analysis of failure cases beyond a few visual examples.

The claimed data-free post-training is still computationally expensive: collecting 50K trajectory pairs and training on 8 H100s for Wan1.3B and 32 H100s for Wan14B is a substantial resource requirement. The paper could better contextualize this cost relative to the gains and to other post-training acceleration methods.

The 15.9-20.9x speedup numbers for the 4-step models are partly due to DMD2 reducing the number of denoising steps, not solely the proposed linear-attention conversion. The paper reports this clearly, but the headline speedup could be misread without careful separation of the two effects.

Baseline coverage is reasonable but not fully satisfying. Some relevant methods are excluded due to training cost, shape constraints, or hardware-specific kernels, and the paper does not report memory usage or scaling behavior across longer videos, batch sizes, or resolutions where linear attention should be most beneficial.

Reproducibility is only partial from the manuscript. The paper gives many hyperparameters, but exact prompt sets, seeds, implementation details for the attention replacement, and code availability are not specified. Given the sensitivity of generative-video evaluation, these details matter.
